stories.title: Big Drug Haul Stopped at Woodlands Checkpoint
stories.headline_kid: A driver tried to sneak more than 10kg of drugs into Singapore hidden in his car — but he got caught!
summary: On Saturday morning, a 22-year-old man drove up to Woodlands Checkpoint, the gate where cars cross from Malaysia into Singapore. Officers from the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) decided to check his car more closely.

Inside, they found about 8.6kg of cannabis and 1.5kg of Ice, also called crystal methamphetamine. That's like carrying dozens of bags of sugar, except instead of sugar, it was dangerous drugs. Both are illegal in Singapore and can seriously harm the brain and body.

The man was arrested on the spot. Singapore has some of the toughest drug laws in the world, and people caught bringing in large amounts of drugs can face very serious punishment, including the death penalty for the most serious cases.

This case shows why checkpoints like Woodlands are so important. Every day, thousands of cars cross the border, and officers work hard to stop dangerous items from entering our country, keeping everyone safer.

lenses.me: It shows why you should never accept a package or bag from a stranger to carry across a border — you could get into serious trouble without even knowing what's inside.
lenses.family: Your family might cross the Woodlands or Tuas checkpoint during holidays, and this story explains why officers sometimes take extra time to check cars carefully.
lenses.friends: If a friend ever jokes about trying drugs, this story is a good reminder of how dangerous and illegal they are in Singapore.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore's checkpoints work hard every day to keep dangerous drugs out of the country.
lenses.world: Drug smuggling is a problem across many countries in the region, and different countries have very different, sometimes extremely strict, punishments for it.

stories.title: Why Your Favourite Soup Might Be Missing Something
stories.headline_kid: Pig blood curd is back in Singapore, but hawkers still can't get enough of it!
summary: Pig blood curd is a soft, dark ingredient found in soups like pig organ soup and kway chap. It was banned for a while, but months ago, Singapore lifted the ban and allowed it back.

The problem is, there's only one factory (called an abattoir) in Thailand that Singapore has approved to send us pig blood curd. That means the supply coming in is much smaller than what hawkers and supermarkets actually need.

Hawkers say they order a certain amount of cartons every week, but they keep receiving fewer than they asked for. This means some stalls might run out of pig blood curd before the day ends, or have to serve smaller portions.

Until more approved factories can supply Singapore, this yummy ingredient may stay hard to find. It's a good example of how food on our plates depends on faraway farms and factories, not just the stall uncle or auntie cooking it.

lenses.me: The next time you order kway chap or pig organ soup, you might notice there's less pig blood curd than usual — now you know why!
lenses.family: Your family might need to try different soup stalls if their usual one has run out of this ingredient.
lenses.friends: If your friends love hawker food, this shows how one small supply problem can affect many stalls across Singapore.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore depends on other countries for some foods, and why food safety rules can affect what's available in our markets.
lenses.world: It's a small example of how global supply chains — the journey food takes from farm to plate — can affect everyday life.

compo_words.example: There is a shortage of pig blood curd across Singapore.

compo_words.meaning: how much people want to buy something
compo_words.example: The demand for pig blood curd is higher than what suppliers can provide.
Only one approved factory can send pig blood curd to Singapore.

compo_phrases.example: The factory could not keep up with demand from Singapore's hawkers.

stories.title: Getting Ready to Keep Schools Safe — Without Making Them Scary
stories.headline_kid: Experts say Singapore should plan ahead in case something bad ever happens at a school, but schools shouldn't turn into fortresses.
summary: Recently, a 14-year-old in Singapore was found to have been influenced by extreme, violent ideas online. He had even recreated shooting scenes in a game called Roblox. Authorities stepped in before anything happened in real life.

This has made experts think carefully about whether Singapore should prepare more seriously for the possibility of an attack at a school one day. A commentary writer explains that being ready doesn't mean turning schools into places with heavy security like airports.

Instead, it means having sensible plans, training teachers, and teaching students and parents to notice worrying signs — like someone talking about hurting others — and speak up early. Schools already do fire drills; this is a similar idea, just for a different kind of danger.

The goal is to keep schools feeling safe and happy places to learn, while still being prepared just in case. Singapore has strong systems, like the Internal Security Department (ISD), that watch out for early warning signs of danger.

lenses.me: If you ever see someone online talking about hurting others, it's always right to tell a trusted adult, even if you're not sure it's serious.
lenses.family: Your parents might notice schools introducing new safety talks or drills — this is part of being prepared, not a sign something bad is about to happen.
lenses.friends: It's a good reminder to be kind to classmates and speak up if a friend seems upset, angry or is saying worrying things.
lenses.nation: Singapore is thinking ahead about school safety so that our schools stay safe places for everyone.
lenses.world: Many countries face similar worries about safety in schools, and are also finding ways to prepare without making children feel scared.

stories.title: Petrol Prices Could Drop as Important Sea Route May Reopen
stories.headline_kid: A big ocean passage that carries lots of the world's oil might reopen soon — and that could mean cheaper petrol for everyone, including Singapore.
summary: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow strip of sea near Iran that huge oil tankers pass through every day. It's like a busy highway, but for ships carrying oil that powers cars, buses and factories all over the world.
For months, tension between the US and Iran caused problems there, making it harder and riskier for ships to pass through. This pushed oil prices up around the world.

But on Tuesday, a US official said a deal to reopen the Strait to shipping could happen very soon — maybe even within a day or two. As soon as people heard this good news, oil prices dropped to their lowest in three weeks, and stock markets went up too.

Singapore doesn't produce its own oil, so we depend on oil shipped in from other countries. If oil becomes cheaper and easier to transport, prices at the petrol pump — and even bus and taxi fares — could eventually become more affordable too.

lenses.me: If your family drives a car, cheaper oil could mean your parents spend less filling up the petrol tank.
lenses.family: Lower oil prices can also make things like cooking gas and even flights slightly cheaper over time.
lenses.friends: Your friends might notice bus or grab fares changing slightly if oil prices keep dropping.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies heavily on imported oil, so news about oil routes reopening directly affects our transport and energy costs.
lenses.world: The Strait of Hormuz is used by ships from many countries, so keeping it open helps keep oil prices stable for the whole world.

compo_words.example: Oil prices plummeted after news of the possible deal.

compo_words.example: The blockage in the Strait had slowed down oil shipments for months.

compo_words.meaning: a raw material or product that is bought and sold, like oil or rice

compo_phrases.example: Shipping through the Strait may soon return back to normal.

stories.title: History on the Court: Alexandra Eala Wins Her First Big Title
stories.headline_kid: Filipino tennis star Alexandra Eala just became the first player from the Philippines to win a WTA Tour title — and tennis fans across Southeast Asia, including Singapore, are cheering!
summary: Alexandra Eala, a 21-year-old tennis player from the Philippines, won her first ever WTA Tour-level singles title at the Washington Open. She beat top seed Jessica Pegula in a thrilling final that was delayed by rain.

The WTA Tour is like the top league for women's professional tennis, similar to how the English Premier League is the top league for football. Winning a title there is a huge deal, especially for a player from Southeast Asia, a region that doesn't often produce top tennis stars.
This win will push Eala up to a career-high ranking of world number 20. Earlier this year, she also caused a stir by beating tennis superstar Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon.

Even though Eala is Filipino and not Singaporean, many young Singaporean tennis fans follow her closely, since she's one of the region's biggest rising stars. Her success shows that athletes from Southeast Asia, including Singapore, can compete — and win — on the world stage.

lenses.me: If you play a sport, Eala's story shows that with hard work, even someone from our region can achieve something amazing on a world stage.
lenses.family: Your family might enjoy watching her future matches together, especially if you're a fan of tennis.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might feel proud watching a fellow Southeast Asian athlete succeed at the highest level.
lenses.nation: Singapore's own young athletes can look up to Eala as an example of a Southeast Asian breaking into a sport usually dominated by other regions.
lenses.world: Her win adds more diversity to women's tennis, showing that talent can come from anywhere in the world.
